description: Dillahunty argues that secular humanists need not presume innate goodness because shared problems and strategic interdependence can generate cooperation, sympathy, and forgiveness without Christianity.
critique: Strongest feature: Dillahunty directly confronts Knechtle’s explanatory claim by separating secular humanism from presumed innate goodness and presenting strategic interdependence as an intelligible alternative source of cooperation, sympathy, and forgiveness. Principal limitation: Invoking “properly applied Game Theory” identifies a relevant framework but supplies neither a concrete mechanism nor comparative evidence showing how reciprocal problem-solving extends to costly out-group concern, sacrificial conduct, sympathy, or forgiveness. Live burden: The rebuttal must demonstrate that strategic interdependence explains the morally demanding phenomena Knechtle emphasized, rather than merely establishing that cooperation can emerge without religious commitment. Locked score: 77 appropriately reflects unusually strong reply contact and substantial relevance while discounting the compressed mechanism, absent examples, and overbroad assertion that these virtues are not Christian functions at all.
